antediluvian

an-tee-dih-LOO-vee-in -- literally 'before the flood' (Latin ante- 'before' + diluvium 'flood'). · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Antediluvian is so old-fashioned it seems almost prehistoric, said to mock or tease rather than to admire.

My uncle still insists his antediluvian rotary phone works just fine.

Example

When the interns discovered the office still used a fax machine, they joked that the whole department must be running on antediluvian technology.

Notice the teasing tone -- nobody actually thinks the fax machine is millions of years old. Antediluvian exaggerates for comic effect, the same way you might call your grandpa's flip phone 'a museum piece.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

outmoded: Outmoded quietly dismisses something as out of style and no longer worth using -- a practical judgment delivered with a shrug, not a joke. Antediluvian goes for the laugh, exaggerating a thing's age until it sounds older than civilization itself.

prehistoric: Prehistoric literally means from the time before written records, and it only sometimes gets borrowed for jokes about old gadgets. Antediluvian has almost given up its literal job: today it exists to tease, mocking something as comically, impossibly ancient.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

modern: belonging to the present time

cutting-edge: the newest and most advanced available

Where it sits · how absurdly out of date it seems — archaic → antediluvian → fossilized

archaic vs. antediluvian: Archaic is milder than antediluvian: an archaic spelling is simply old and out of use, noted with a straight face, while antediluvian piles on comic exaggeration to mock something as absurdly ancient.

fossilized vs. antediluvian: Fossilized is stronger than antediluvian: an antediluvian fax machine is only teased for its age, but a fossilized bureaucracy is accused of having hardened so completely that it can never change at all.

Which word fits?

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — ante-

prefix — ante-: before (Latin)

root — -diluv-

root — -diluv-: flood (Latin (diluvium))

suffix — -ian

suffix — -ian: relating to (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Antediluvian comes from Latin ante- ('before') plus diluvium ('flood') plus -ian ('relating to') -- literally 'relating to the time before the flood,' as in Noah's flood. Calling something antediluvian jokingly suggests it is so old it predates practically everything.

Use the root in a new word: deluge

Use the root in a new word: deluge: A deluge of complaints flooded the customer service line within minutes of the price increase.

Word Building

Word Choice

Antediluvian is almost always used with a wink -- for comic exaggeration, not literal history. Compare "bygone," which has a gentler, nostalgic tone with no mockery, and "antecedent," which isn't really about 'old' at all but about what came before and caused something later.
